claims.text: The relevant protective coating has an interpenetrating or lamellar dual-phase FCC/BCC (or FCC/B2-like) microstructure.
The BCC phase is harder than the FCC phase.
The FCC/BCC interfaces are coherent or semi-coherent.
FCC/BCC interfaces pin dislocations and impede their motion.
An interconnected BCC phase acts as an anchoring network against deformation.
The BCC phase has higher lattice friction and greater inherent resistance to dislocation glide than the FCC phase.
Applied stress causes FCC dislocations to be hindered at FCC/BCC interfaces, delaying dislocation nucleation and motion.
Dislocation bypass of the BCC network and its interfaces requires increased energy.
The dual-phase microstructure elevates the activation energy for creep deformation.
Stress and temperature significantly affect creep mechanisms, and sufficiently high stress can lead from diffusion-dominated creep to dislocation activity and eventually phase transformation.
The interface-mediated benefit operates below the yield limit and below temperatures or stresses that compromise phase stability.
A dual-phase FCC/BCC coating has greater creep resistance than a comparable single-phase FCC coating.
The dual-phase coating will exhibit a significantly lower creep strain rate than the single-phase FCC baseline.
The dual-phase coating will undergo less progressive macroscopic plastic deformation than the single-phase FCC baseline.
After creep testing, dislocation activity will be concentrated near FCC/BCC phase boundaries.
Eutectic alloy design and controlled solidification can produce a fine lamellar FCC/BCC or FCC/B2 microstructure.
Processing modifications can produce an otherwise compositionally identical single-phase FCC control for the dual-phase coating.
